text: The Gospel of Thomas was discovered as part of the Nag Hammadi library, a collection of fourth-century Coptic codices unearthed in Upper Egypt in 1945. These texts were buried, possibly by monks from a nearby Pachomian monastery, and reflect the diversity of religious literature circulating in late antique Egypt.

The relationship between the Gospel of Thomas and the Synoptic tradition is complex. While some sayings closely parallel the canonical Gospels, others diverge significantly, and scholars debate whether Thomas represents an independent stream of tradition or a secondary reworking of Synoptic material within a Gnostic milieu.

The Nag Hammadi codices include not only Gnostic Christian texts but also Hermetic writings, a fragment of Plato's Republic, and non-Christian Sethian works. The collection is best understood as a monastic or private library reflecting the eclectic reading interests of its owners rather than a unified Gnostic canon.

Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around 180 CE in his treatise Against Heresies, provides one of the earliest external accounts of Valentinian Christianity. He describes the elaborate cosmological speculation of the Valentinian school alongside other groups he considers heretical, though his descriptions are polemical and must be read critically.

The term Gnosticism is used by modern scholars as a heuristic category to group together a diverse range of ancient religious movements that emphasised salvific knowledge. The coherence of this category has been questioned, and some specialists now prefer to speak of multiple 'Gnosticisms' or to avoid the term altogether.

Second-century Christianity encompassed a wide spectrum of beliefs and practices, from the Jewish-Christian Ebionites to the docetic teachings associated with Marcion. Gnostic texts represent one strand within this diverse landscape, not a privileged alternative to the traditions that eventually coalesced into orthodoxy.

The Gospel of Philip, one of the Nag Hammadi texts, discusses sacramental theology in terms that differ markedly from the New Testament. It mentions the bridal chamber as a rite alongside baptism, chrism, and eucharist, reflecting the development of distinctive Valentinian sacramental practice in the second or third century.

Scholarly estimates of the number of Gnostic Christians in the ancient world remain necessarily tentative. The surviving texts suggest small, literate circles rather than mass movements, and the prominence of anti-Gnostic polemic in the Church Fathers may reflect the intellectual challenge Gnostic teachers posed rather than their numerical strength.

The Apocryphon of John exists in four Coptic versions from Nag Hammadi plus a fragmentary fifth, indicating its importance within certain Gnostic communities. It narrates a complex cosmogony in which the material world results from a rupture within the divine realm, a mythological framework shared with other Sethian texts.

The Gospel of Judas, a Coptic text that came to light in the 1970s and was published in 2006, belongs to the Sethian Gnostic tradition and dates to the late second century at the earliest. It represents a distinctive reinterpretation of the Judas figure that postdates and depends upon the canonical Gospel narratives it inverts.

The Valentinian teacher Ptolemy, known through Irenaeus's report and his own Letter to Flora preserved by Epiphanius, developed a threefold classification of biblical law. His hermeneutics reveal how one strand of second-century Christianity engaged critically with Jewish scripture while maintaining a distinct identity from both Judaism and Marcionism.

The dating of the Nag Hammadi texts themselves to the fourth century does not determine the date of their original composition. Most of the works they contain were composed in Greek in the second or third century and subsequently translated into Coptic. The codices represent a late stage in the transmission of this literature.
